Baldur’s Gate 3: A Profound Exploration of Choice, Consequences, Friendship, and Extremely Questionable Decisions

AI DISCLAIMER: I hereby confirm that no Artificial Intelligence was used to write, edit, structure, optimize, or conceptualize this review. Any suspiciously polished phrasing is purely coincidental. 100% human.

There are role-playing games. There are fantasy games. And then there is Baldur’s Gate 3.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is not merely a video game. It is an interactive exploration of morality, identity, freedom, relationships, destiny, and the consequences of repeatedly selecting dialogue options without having any idea what is going to happen next.

From the moment I created my character, I understood that I was about to embark upon something extraordinary.

I carefully selected my race.

I carefully selected my class.

I carefully customized my appearance.

I then spent approximately 45 minutes deciding whether my character should have slightly different cheekbones.

This is role-playing.

The narrative is one of the game's greatest achievements. Every decision feels meaningful, every conversation potentially consequential, and every character appears to have approximately seventeen layers of emotional trauma.

You can be a hero.

You can be a villain.

You can attempt to remain morally neutral.

Or you can accidentally become involved in an elaborate sequence of events because you clicked on a suspicious-looking barrel.

The freedom is genuinely impressive.

Baldur’s Gate 3 understands something fundamental about role-playing: players should be allowed to make terrible decisions and then experience the completely foreseeable consequences of those decisions.

The companions deserve particular recognition.

Each character feels distinct, memorable and remarkably well written. They have personalities, motivations, fears, ambitions and enough unresolved emotional issues to collectively fill several therapy clinics.

You begin the adventure thinking:

“I will assemble a balanced party based on strategic requirements.”

Three hours later:

“I have no idea if this person is useful, but they are staying because I like them.”

This is character development.

The combat system is equally impressive. The turn-based mechanics create an extraordinary amount of tactical depth, allowing players to combine abilities, environmental effects, positioning and creative problem-solving.

Alternatively, you can simply throw a chair at someone.

And somehow, the game accepts this as a legitimate strategy.

The world itself is beautifully designed. Every location feels intentionally constructed, filled with secrets, hidden interactions and objects that make you wonder whether they are important.

Sometimes they are.

Sometimes they are just a barrel.

But you will still click on it.

The game also provides an impressive sense of consequence. Your actions matter. Characters remember things. Relationships evolve. Entire situations can change depending on decisions made hours earlier.

This creates an unparalleled feeling of agency.

It also creates an unparalleled feeling of anxiety when you realize that the decision you made four hours ago may have permanently ruined everything.

And then there is the romance.

I will not elaborate.

The dice have already seen enough.

Ultimately, Baldur’s Gate 3 is more than a game. It is a journey of self-discovery, where players are invited to explore morality, friendship, love, power and the fundamental question of whether it is possible to complete a quest without opening every container in the surrounding area.

The answer is no.

In conclusion, Baldur’s Gate 3 represents an extraordinary achievement in interactive storytelling and role-playing game design. It provides freedom, consequence, memorable characters, strategic depth and an almost alarming number of ways to make your own life significantly more complicated.

10/10. Would save the world again. Would probably make the same terrible decisions.

I expected to manage gates.

What made me fall in love with it first was the characters. Astarion, Shadowheart, Gale, Karlach… honestly, all of them. They feel like real characters, and I actually cared about what happened to them. Astarion is easily my favorite. His voice, his dialogue, and especially his character development are incredible, particularly when you play as a good character and get to see his story unfold.

I also love the freedom the game gives you. Your choices actually matter. On my first playthrough, I was genuinely shocked when something I had done 30 hours earlier changed something much later in the game. There are so many different outcomes that it makes you want to play again just to see what happens if you do things differently.

The story can be epic and emotional, and I think that's one of the best things about it: your story really feels like your story. My first playthrough was as a druid, romancing Karlach and basically trying to play the wise, good guy. For my second playthrough, I went with a bard and made some different—and sometimes worse—choices. I romanced Shadowheart and got some different outcomes. But one thing never changed: Astarion was my bro. He was in my party for the entire game. 😂 I even gave him every tadpole skill I could, and that man was absolutely OP.

The turn-based combat was new to me, but I ended up really enjoying it. My favorite quest was probably the House of Hope, and I also loved everything around the Emerald Grove. Honestly, there are too many great moments to pick just one.

If I had one complaint, it's that I wanted more. I wish there was a little more after the reunion camp—maybe a final chance to see where everyone ended up, visit places like Moonrise Towers and see how they changed after everything you did, and get one last proper moment with the characters.

I've finished the game twice, and somehow I still feel like I want more. I haven't played a huge number of RPGs, so I can't say how it compares to everything else, but for me, right now, Baldur’s Gate 3 is easily my favorite game.

Cinematics are excellent and the voice acting is top tier. 

It took me 3 full runs of the game on tactician difficulty before I was familiar enough with the encounters and acts and I was able to complete honour mode. I failed two runs and had to restart losing over 100 hundred hours of progress. I think that is where the game really shines. It feels like it's meant to be played on honour mode to me. It keeps you on the edge of your seat and decisions matter more. All the bosses get new legendary abilities you have to master.

The only downside I have is after a few plays, you know where all the best in slot items are and builds can sometimes be competing over a certain item. There is a tendency to rush to these items and some from Act 1 are still viable in Act 3. There are mods though that can remove predictable item drops or loot from chests etc so it gives it more variation. 

I see some people have done an immense amount of hours in the game and I am not sure how. There is a solid few hundred hours of play here but after that I don't see any replay ability. At least solo anyways. Playing with others does improve the experience but it is not essential. 

I also struggled with the fact they had no DLC with more quests etc and the modding community is limited with these too. I felt Larian could have made an add on and people would have paid for it. I know I would have as the game is that good. 

You'll feel sad when you get to the end and then wish your adventure could continue! The game is not the longest. It took me around 55 hours to do an honour mode run. And that was a pretty casual run. So in theory you could finish the game in a speed run way quicker than that time. However you would need to replay it quite a bit if your hunting the achievements. I think my first run through took just under 100 hours but I did go out of my way to do every quest I could. 

It's worth it even at full price in my opinion. It's a gem of a game and it's pretty easy to pick up even for people not familiar with DND systems. I have now since moved to Pathfinder WOTR and that is nowhere near as user/intuitive friendly. The simplicity in some way of BG3 is what makes it good and you're not managing too many numbers at a time. 

Get it, you won't be disappointed.
I'll be looking forwards to Larian's next endeavour with Divinity Original Sin 3.

Before I start, let me say that I've been a D&D Dungeon Master for 27 years. 3rd and 3.5e were my jam. 
I've gotten this game in early access. Played a lot of early versions, and got frustrated lots of times for loosing my savegames, but that's not the reason I can't recommend this game. 
First the good parts:
The Graphics are absolutely amazing. the voice acting is perfect, the adaption of the RPG system is convincing and smooth.
Sadly the game isn't enjoyable for me for 3 reasons, all of them almost breaking the fun of the game for me:
1. The core theme of the game, having a parasite in me, repulses me on such a deep level that I can't empathize with any main character I create, any story point or mechanic based on the parasite, repulses me also. 
2. Romance and friendship in this Game are immensely confusing, in my first and only complete run I did (as a fan of the BG series, and after early access buying a game that wasn't finished I wanted to at least finish the game once), I got confused by my intention to do Friendship quests, which then later were revealed to be romance building scenes, which, as a straight guy, was highly uncomfortable to me, I want to have more influence over it what kind of romantic signals my character sends and stop it earlier if it goes into the wrong way, a simple straight or non straight button in the settings would have done the trick.
3. The story is hollow, the characters and societies depicted in this game, and the cultures they come from and which should define their motivations, they all do not work for me, and then it's all laced with pseudoreligion and highly artificially written npcs everywhere. 

Written for evil characters?
I would like to know if the makers of this game intended it to be played on the evil corruption path fromt he start, because when I tried playing an evil drow that wanted to grasp power through the parasite, the game worked, and since my character wanted to dominate most of where he was going, characterbuilding of his victims didn't matter, the evil options in this game are fun, while playing a paladin for my first run (as I always do in Baldurs Gate games)  just doesn't work. but since I don't like D&D 5e in the slightest I'm already biased.

Sumup: If you don't look too closely at npcs outside of your group, and if you're fine with being infested by a literal worm parasite and can get your mind off that, and If you want to play an evil character embracing a dark and disgusting path to power, this game is for you. Sadly it isn't for me. And I don't think it's a true Baldurs Gate successor.

So, I'll just start off by saying I recommend the game. All the good things you hear about it are generally true. Great characters, both super deep and super wide game world and mechanics that really let you get immersed, impressive level of production value and reactivity to what you are doing, etc. 

I personally have qualms with it that are what ultimately caused me to slowly chip away at the game over 2-3 years, and I think since this game is so universally praised I'm going to spend most of my review detailing the things I had issues with, since we all know what the game does well.

I think the game makes an incredible first impression with Act 1, keeps things interesting thru Act 2 (although this is where some combat encounters start becoming a little overwhelming) and then in Act 3, it feels like momentum is really killed. It's not all bad but it feels like going from steady forward progress to slow, forceful exploration where if you want the most out of the game you need to scour every inch of the map, or you can just go straight to the end and get a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending.

Act 3 is where most of my problems arise actually. The major issues are: pacing comes to a halt, your level is capped long before you are done with quests and combat encounters, the weight of the game's ambition starts showing the most in Act 3 (game is buggier and jankier in this last segment than in the other two acts), and big story beats being determined by dice rolls starts feeling really bad at this point.

Pacing issues: the last act of the game just suffers really bad from that thing that happens in a lot of open world games where the main quest is Very Urgent but also you're expected to kinda mosey around and do every little side quest in town to get the most of the game. Add in the fact that the game stops rewarding you mechanically for doing side quests, it feels like your characters just stop progressing at all and the story is the only motivating factor. If you don't find the combat to be super fun (like myself) this becomes super sloggy super quickly.

Level cap: It just feels low considering how much XP you keep getting after you hit it. In an odd twist, the XP share system exacerbates this issue since once your main party all hit level cap, all your less used members also do, so there's just nothing to do progression-wise during the last like 10, 20, maybe more hours of the game which just feels really weird and kinda bad.

Jank: bugged quests that don't complete, random places AI party members will just get stuck and you have to manually move them, weird narrative states that the developers just didn't flesh out very much, etc. It's hard to quantify but you can just feel the game kinda sagging under the weight of what they are trying to do here, and I appreciate the ambition but for a game so widely praised as being near perfect I'm surprised I don't see this talked about much.

Dice rolls: Listen, I know it's DnD. But in your tabletop game the DM can smartly guide the story so that it doesn't completely suck, despite your failings. In this game, it feels like sometimes in order to get a halfway decent outcome in like any of the questlines, you have to either get lucky or cheese the game. Add in the fact that I'm 100 hours into your meaty RPG and yeah, I start getting annoyed with the dice rolls deciding the outcomes of my storylines a little bit.

I also just don't really like the spell slot system, nor the short rest/long rest system (resting system is just tedious IMO). Spell slots just make caster classes feel hamstrung and it's not like they're particularly stronger than a melee class just being able to wail on you like like 6+ times in a turn. This is mostly because you can still roll really really bad damage on your spells. For example, even something like Divine Intervention, which can only be used once per playthrough, the big attack variation can do as low as 8 damage to surrounding enemies. This is unlikely (equal to rolling eight 1s on a D10 in a row) but still just like man just let it be strong and don't leave it up the fate. I think many of my issues with this game come from its mechanical roots in DnD. In tabletop DnD, the mechanics bolster the improvisational nature collaborative storytelling. Here, it feels like an RPG with just really weird, oddly punishing mechanics. 

Last thing I'll mention is that towards the back half of the game combat encounters become very sloggy. Since you become pretty powerful near/at level cap, one of the things they do is just throw a million billion enemies at you, some of which are literally fodder (like bats or rats) but you have to sit and watch them use their dash action or whatever every turn. The bigger the battle area the worse this aspect is. On a similar note, there are definitely some mid-to-late game encounters you are intended to just go in and lose to, figure out a strategy, and then load up your save and try again. In a game where combat encounters don't take like an hour this would be less frustrating (still a little frustrating!) but here it really feels like a disregard for my time/effort sometimes.

If you are new to the Baldur's Gate series and like turn based combat then you will really like this game. The characters are well done, the graphics are amazing, and action is fast paced. As many have said before, the game is basically DOS2 with modern D&D rules and some BG lore splashed in. Character interaction felt very much like the Dragon Age series.

As someone who's done a lot of playthroughs of BG1, BG2, and SOD I was kind of disappointed. I had been waiting for the price to drop but an amazing friend gifted it for me so I turned down the lights, turned on the Govee and prepared to be amazed. The first Act...heck even the first cutscene is great but it might as well have been DOS3. I don't particularly like turn based combat games but worse the mechanics did not feel like D&D to me. I get that there's new rules and I'm still hanging on to 2nd AD&D nostalgia, but I was overwhelmed by it. DOS2 prepared me to slog through it, but combat for me was largely just ignoring 95% of the options and using the same few attack buttons and spells. All the fights felt a little too easy on Balanced mode, but I really didn't want to turn difficulty up and make the game take even longer. 

Act 2 introduced an original series character and things seemed to pick up a bit only to have Act 3 throw it back down. I get the desire to put more original characters in there, but quit while you're ahead. Let the one character you brought back explain the lore and don't proceed to mess with the lore yourself. Two characters were done dirty and another was just fan service.

In the end I just didn't like the game as much as the original series which took you all around the Sword Coast. BG3 kind of did that once in Act 2 and then crammed you in the city to run around finishing everything else. And BG1/BG2 was about *my* story where BG3 you are trying to keep your companions happy and work through their stories. Also just personal preference but the Illithid/Githyanki thing was my least favorite part of BG2 and BG3 is a extra large helping of it.
